issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never Alone' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence and the rest of the profile. This item more strongly suggests fear of being alone with a potentially abusive intimate or familiar person, whereas the threat items center on strangers and general vigilance. That mismatch is difficult to explain clinically within the same trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is not well aligned with the trauma type and accompanying appraisals. Feeling dirty or contaminated is more characteristic of sexual trauma; with police violence, and with the current memory/threat content, this appraisal stands out as clinically incongruent rather than merely unusual.

vignette:
Daniel had built his adult life around order, competence, and the quiet routines of his dental practice, so the night he was stopped by police and brought into a frightening confrontation with force felt to him like a total rupture. He had been in his own city, in an ordinary public setting, when what began as a routine encounter escalated into police violence that left him overwhelmed, humiliated, and physically shaken. In the days that followed, he found himself replaying the scene not as something that had happened to him, but almost as if it belonged to someone else, as though he were watching another man endure it. Yet it was never fully distant. When the memory came back, certain sounds returned with it in a jarring, involuntary way, and he would hear fragments of what had been said in his mind as though the voices were still in the room. At those moments, he also noticed the same bodily pain in the parts of his body that had been hurt during the event, a sharp reminder that made the memory feel immediate and physical rather than past.

Daniel, who is 58 and in a long-term relationship, had once taken pride in being composed and self-contained, but after the incident he became wary of almost anything that might stir feeling of any kind. He was careful to keep himself busy and to avoid situations, conversations, or memories that might bring on either sadness or relief, because both felt dangerous to him. He came to arrange his days around not being overwhelmed. What had once been an active, social rhythm became narrowed and guarded. He was also determined to avoid stress wherever possible, and that made his world smaller in practical ways. He turned down tasks and commitments that would have added pressure, and he began to protect himself by reducing exposure to anything unpredictable.

The change was especially visible in public. Daniel, who worked as a dentist and spent long hours in clinical spaces, started to scan every environment constantly, taking in entrances, faces, and movement before he could settle. In restaurants, waiting rooms, and other everyday places, he automatically chose the seat that felt safest or most protected, often positioning himself with his back to a wall or a clear view of the room. He did this without needing to explain it, simply because he felt exposed otherwise. Strangers approaching him, even in ordinary situations, became a source of immediate threat in his mind. A person walking toward him on a sidewalk, someone stopping too close in a lobby, or an unfamiliar face entering his space could make him tense and alert before he could reason with himself. At night, the same vigilance followed him into bed. He struggled to fall asleep and, when he did sleep, he often woke and found himself listening for signs of danger, unable to fully let go.

In his dental office, Daniel’s distress became harder to conceal. The predictable structure of appointments helped him function, but even there he found himself monitoring the surroundings more than he had before, checking the waiting area and the doorway between patients. He noticed that sitting in his own office chair no longer felt neutral; he chose positions in the room based on how protected he felt, as though danger could enter at any moment. The demands of the practice, which had once felt manageable, now carried an added strain because he was trying so hard to stay controlled and to avoid anything that might upset him. Over time, colleagues and his partner noticed that he had become more withdrawn and less willing to engage in the kinds of spontaneous conversations and activities that had once come easily.

Daniel’s beliefs about the event were marked by a harsh sense of personal blame and injustice. He had come to believe there was something about him that made it happen, some flaw or weakness that marked him out for what occurred, even though he could not clearly name what that was. At the same time, he felt that what had happened was profoundly unfair and that nothing had been done about it. That combination left him angry, resentful, and exhausted, while also convinced that the life he had known had been fundamentally damaged. He spoke of it as though his life had been destroyed by the trauma, not in a dramatic way, but with the weary certainty of someone who felt his assumptions about safety, fairness, and his own place in the world had been permanently altered.

He eventually sought help when the strain of keeping everything contained became too difficult to manage. The constant scanning, the sleep disruption, the avoidance of people and stress, and the growing sense that he could not simply push through it had begun to interfere with his daily functioning and his relationship. He now wants relief from the relentless sense of threat and from the way the memory can suddenly return with sound, pain, and a sense of unreality. More than anything, Daniel hopes to feel safe enough in his own body and in ordinary public spaces to live without measuring every seat, every stranger, and every room for danger.
